Conclusions Current microbiome methodologies present challenges with samples of low microbial biomass, making it difficult to detect bacterial signals that are distinct or above levels found in collection and processing environments. Of concern is the lack of precision and reproducibility with samples of low microbial biomass. Technical replicates, alternative sequencing strategies, and absolute quantification of bacterial DNA should be used to confirm the reliability of microbiome sequencing data from low biomass samples. This study provides important insights into site-specific microbiomes from lung cancer patients and the challenges encountered when assessing the tumour microbiome.

title: From under-ice accumulation to open-water oxidation: microbial regulation of methane emissions in high-altitude proglacial lakes
abstract: Proglacial lakes, formed by global warming and accelerating deglaciation, represent widespread yet poorly constrained sources of methane (CH 4 ). Although their emissions are closely associated with ice-cover and ice-free conditions, the microbial mechanisms underlying these dynamics are not understood. Here, we integrated multi-season field observations, stable isotope analyses, metagenomic sequencing, and incubation experiments to investigate microbial controls on seasonal CH 4 cycling in newly formed high-altitude proglacial lakes on the Tibetan Plateau. We observed substantial accumulation of dissolved CH 4 in the water column even during the ice-covered period (ICP), despite the enrichment of anaerobic methanotrophs (Candidatus Methylomirabilota) in sediments. Isotope analysis showed that CH 4 oxidation was active during the early ICP but became limited during the late ICP, leading to continued CH 4 accumulation. Following the transition to the ablation period (AP), acetoclastic methanogenesis ( Methanosarcina ) rapidly recovered in bottom sediments. Concurrently, significant aerobic methanotrophy ( Methylobacter ) was established in surface sediments. Temperature was strongly associated with the shift of methanogenic and methanotrophic communities from the ICP to the AP. This microbial reorganization was accompanied by an increased relative abundance of CH 4 metabolism genes and enhanced functional coupling among CH 4 , nitrogen, and sulfur cycling pathways. Overall, our findings demonstrate that microbial succession contributes to the seasonal transition from net CH 4 accumulation beneath the ice to net CH 4 consumption during open-water conditions. Given the potentially greater temperature sensitivity of methanogenesis relative to methanotrophy, continued climate warming may disrupt the balance, potentially transforming rapidly expanding proglacial lakes into stronger sources of atmospheric CH 4 . Video Abstract

title: Lung microbiota dysbiosis exacerbates influenza virus infection
abstract: BACKGROUND: Previous studies have shown that microbiota in the respiratory tract play a significant role in shaping host immunity and reducing the risk of respiratory tract infections. Influenza, an acute respiratory infectious disease caused by the influenza virus (IAV), necessitates to have an in-depth understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms of viral infection and to utilize these mechanisms to prevent and control influenza infection. RESULTS: In this study, we established models of different disease severity levels in mice infected with IAV, the relationships between changes in pulmonary microbiota and host interactions during IAV infection were analyzed. We found that these relationships were characterized by the enrichment of opportunistic pathogenic taxonomic groups and were related to disease severity. Multi-omics analysis combined with animal experiments clarified that colonization of Bacillus cereus in the lungs aggravates IAV infection through xanthosine, thereby downregulating the expression of nt5e and reducing the viral phagocytic ability of alveolar macrophages. Importantly, targeted removal of B. cereus by bacteriophages can alleviate IAV infection and the resulting pulmonary lesions. CONCLUSIONS: Highlighting provides a novel approach for preventing and controlling the progression of IAV infection by targeting the lung microbiota. IN BRIEF: Lung dysbiosis is associated with severe influenza virus (IAV) infection. Bacillus cereus aggravates IAV infection via the xanthosine-nt5e axis in SPF mice, which can be rescued by bacteriophage targeting. These findings highlight the potential of modulating the lung microbiota as a strategy for prevention and controlling IAV infection.

title: TrIdent—an R package to automate transductomics analysis of virus-like particle mediated DNA mobilization
abstract: Background: Transduction is a form of horizontal gene transfer in which bacterial DNA is packaged and transferred by virus-like particles (VLPs). Transductomics is a sequencing-based method used to detect DNA carried by VLPs. During transductomics analysis, reads from a sample's ultra-purified VLPs are mapped to metagenomic contigs assembled from the same sample's whole-community. The read mapping produces coverage patterns that require a time-consuming manual inspection and classification process which makes the method's use unfeasible for datasets with many samples. Results: ification), that uses pattern-matching to automate the transductomics data analysis and that is available as an R package (https://jlmaier12.github.io/TrIdent/). There is no software equivalent to TrIdent so we compared TrIdent's classifications of transductomics datasets to classifications made by human classifiers. TrIdent's classifications were generally comparable to the manual classifications on a previously generated, manually classified transductomics dataset. When applied to newly generated transductomics data from the murine microbiota, TrIdent agreed with two independent human classifiers as much as the two independent human classifications agreed with each other. TrIdent classified transductomics datasets in a fraction of the time needed by human classifiers, and the classifications produced by TrIdent are fully reproducible. We used TrIdent to explore three murine gut transductomes and found that bacterial DNA associated with the Oscillospiraceae and Turicibacteraceae families was highly enriched in the DNA packaged by VLPs as compared to the whole community metagenomes. Conclusions: The TrIdent software is a more accessible, more efficient, and more reproducible alternative to the manual inspection of read coverage patterns previously required for transductomics data analysis. To demonstrate the application of TrIdent, we analyzed transductomics datasets from murine fecal pellets and showed that specific low abundance bacterial families appear to be heavily involved in transduction.

title: Sex-specific effects of early-life arsenic exposure on body weight, arsenic metabolism, and gut microbiome stability in C57BL/6J mice
abstract: Arsenic exposure in early-life is strongly linked to health risks for mothers and their offspring. Although the mechanisms by which arsenic induces the toxicity and health impacts remain unclear, the gut microbiome makes key contributions to the metabolism of arsenic. This study established a C57BL/6 mice model of pregnancy to explore the impact of exposure to environmental concentrations of arsenic on growth and gut microbiome dynamics in pregnant mice and their offspring. Maternal exposure to 0.10 mg/L arsenic during gestation (initiated at GD0 and GD14, respectively) and lactation elevated gut microbial diversity in pups at 3 weeks of age, with body weight markedly decreasing in the GD0 group but significantly increasing in the GD14 group. Compared to pups receiving solely a 5-week high-dose arsenic exposure (10.0 mg/L) during adolescence, those with early-life low-dose followed by the same adolescent high-dose exposure exhibited sex-specific alterations in gut microbiome and arsenic metabolism. At 8 weeks of age, this exposure promoted gut microbial diversity and network interactions in female pups, concurrently downregulating As V reduction genes and reducing kidney arsenic bioaccumulation. By contrast, male pups exhibited divergent responses, where arsenic exposure decreased microbial diversity and network interactions, accompanied by increased feces arsenic excretion and decreased liver arsenic bioaccumulation. This study highlights the short- and long-term impact of arsenic exposure on gut microbiome stability and the arsenic metabolic characteristics under different exposure conditions, which offers novel insights into the developmental toxicity of arsenic exposure in early life. Video Abstract

title: Error control for microbiome mediation analysis: benchmarking and remedy
abstract: Abstract Background Identifying microbial taxa that mediate the effects of exposures on health outcomes can elucidate causal pathways and suggest therapeutic targets. Microbiome sequencing typically measures relative abundances (RA) of taxa, while absolute abundances (AA)—often the relevant scale for mechanistic interpretation—are not directly observed. Although compositionality-induced false positives have been documented in other microbiome analyses (e.g., differential abundance testing), systematic benchmarking of microbiome mediation methods remains scarce. Results We benchmarked nine mediation methods using extensive simulations and a real data application. We anchor our simulations to an experimentally derived AA template dataset, generating AA profiles that better preserve empirical structure than commonly used simulators. Across simulation settings, many methods exhibit inflated error rates, with inflation worsening as compositional effects intensify. In the real data application, methods exhibiting severe inflation in simulations also returned substantially larger mediator sets. As a remedy, we introduce CAMRA, which infers and tests AA-level mediation effects from standard RA data. CAMRA improves FDR calibration and power for taxon-level mediator discovery while maintaining favorable runtime. Conclusions Reliable microbial mediator discovery requires well-calibrated inference. Our benchmark highlights systematic challenges for RA-level mediation testing. CAMRA offers a remedy by targeting AA-level mediation effects.

title: Viable microbial ecology and functional potential of the Integrated Lunar-Mars Analog Habitat revealed by multi-omics analyses
abstract: Long-duration human missions to the Moon and Mars will rely on closed, self-sustaining habitats where microorganisms inevitably interact with crew, materials, and life-support systems. While routine cleaning and environmental control can limit microbial growth, viable populations may persist and adapt to resource limitation, environmental parameter fluctuations, and disinfection stress. Distinguishing living from dead biomass is therefore essential for risk assessment. However, few studies have examined the viable microbiome of confined, human-occupied analogs using multi-omics, viability-targeted approaches. Across a 21-day continuous-occupation trial in the Integrated Lunar-Mars Analog Habitat (ILMAH), propidium monoazide-treated digital PCR (PMA-dPCR) assay results revealed strong spatial heterogeneity in viable bacterial loads (10 8 to 10 11 16S rRNA gene copies m − 2 ), with consistently higher burdens in high-traffic modules (Entrance, Kitchen, Bathroom, Crew Quarters) than low-traffic modules (Welch’s Δ = 4.11 log₁₀; p < 0.001; ANOVA F₇,₃₂ = 6.7, p < 0.001). Viable fungal loads were more uniform and did not differ by location ( p = 0.38). Intracellular ATP tracked viable microorganisms and correlated with PMA-dPCR across modules, whereas culture counts determined using “ready-to-use dry-sheet culture media” were 2–3 logs lower, consistent with a substantial viable but nonculturable fraction. From 240 isolates, 140 bacteria and 100 fungi were characterized; 42 bacterial and 26 fungal species were identified, including three putative novel fungal taxa. Microbiome characterization using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing from PMA-treated samples showed location-driven community structure (PERMANOVA p = 0.021) dominated by Pseudomonas , with episodic Acinetobacter enrichment in low-traffic areas. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed strong spatial structuring of viable microbiomes, with high-traffic modules enriched in Pseudomonas , while low-traffic modules showed increased fungal prevalence and greater taxonomic diversity. Metagenomics further detected low-abundance viable biosafety level-2 taxa (e.g., Salmonella enterica , Serratia species) and concentrated antimicrobial resistance genes and virulence factor signatures in high-traffic modules, largely carried by Pseudomonas . The ILMAH habitat supports a spatially differentiated, stress-tolerant core microbiome maintained by human occupancy and selective survival. Viability-based assays reveal that while total DNA may overestimate viable microbial diversity, the living community is low in richness yet high in resilience. This integrative workflow establishes a foundation for biosurveillance and microbial-risk management in future long-duration spaceflight and other sealed ecological systems. Video Abstract

title: Functional division between root endosphere and rhizosphere microbiomes supports seagrass holobiont resilience under high nutrient and sulfide exposure
abstract: Coastal eutrophication leads to the co-occurrence of high nutrient loading and sulfide exposure, posing severe threats to the health of seagrass ecosystems. Yet the underlying adaptive mechanisms of the seagrass holobiont remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a large-scale field investigation along a tropical natural gradient of nutrient and sulfide to examine the adaptive mechanisms of seagrass holobiont. By integrating plant physiology, stable isotopes, metabolomics, 16S rRNA amplicon, and shotgun metagenomics, we particularly explored the interaction between seagrass host and associated microbiome. The seagrass host exhibited physiological and metabolic patterns consistent with a growth-defense trade-off, with high nutrient conditions showing a more growth-related metabolite profile and sulfide exposure coinciding with a stronger antioxidant defense-related metabolite profile. The metabolic reprogramming was accompanied by changes in the relative abundance of several root exudates, including flavonoids and phenylpropanoids, rather than a significant bulk compositional shift. These differential exudates showed compartment-specific relationships with microbiome composition, with nitrogen-cycling taxa preferentially associated with the root endosphere under high nutrient conditions and sulfur-cycling taxa preferentially enriched in the rhizosphere under sulfide exposure. Notably, this putative functional division of labor appeared to be reconfigured under dual pressure, with endosphere communities showing greater representation of taxa putatively related to sulfur cycling. In addition, the rhizosphere microbiome showed stressor-tailored genomic potential, with sulfur oxidation and transfer related genes (e.g., fccBA and dsrEF ) more prominent under sulfide exposed conditions and redundant ammonia assimilation potential (e.g., gltD) under nutrient-enriched conditions, potentially relevant to nutrient stress mitigation. This work suggests that seagrass holobiont resilience to co-occurring nutrient and sulfide exposure may be associated with host changes in root exudation and compartmentalized microbiome functional potential. We propose that the putative functional division of root microbiota provides a useful ecological framework for developing microbiome-informed seagrass restoration and conservation strategies. Video Abstract

title: Temperature-dependent phage-bacterium coexistence strategy mediates the intestinal microbial community diversity in shrimp
abstract: The diversity of intestinal bacterial communities is closely associated with host health. Phage-bacterium interactions are key determinants of this diversity, and temperature represents a critical environmental factor influencing these interactions. At elevated temperatures, pathogenic bacteria such as Vibrio parahaemolyticus ( V. parahaemolyticus ) proliferate in shrimp aquaculture systems, whereas phages with density-dependent infection dynamics fail to control bacterial populations, resulting in recurrent digestive tract diseases. In this study, a V. parahaemolyticus -T6 (VP) strain and its lytic phage (VP-T6a) were isolated from the shrimp intestine. Integrated omics analyses were employed to investigate how temperature modulates phage- V. parahaemolyticus interactions during infection and how these temperature-dependent dynamics affect intestinal microbial diversity. In vitro, VP-T6a replicated efficiently at relatively low temperatures (20°C–33°C), increasing its abundance, reducing VP density, and elevating the multiplicity of infection (MOI). However, phage-resistant VP variants emerged during co-culture with VP-T6a, preventing complete lysis of the VP population. At higher temperatures (35°C–37°C), the expression of VP-T6a packaging-related genes was suppressed after adsorption to VP, resulting in no production of progeny phages. Consequently, VP continued to replicate normally, increasing in abundance, whereas VP-T6a abundance declined, leading to a lower MOI. Within the optimal MOI range (0.001–0.01), co-cultures of VP-T6a and VP yielded the highest titers of progeny phages. In vivo, temperature also modulated VP-T6a-VP interactions within the shrimp intestine. The two temperature-dependent interaction patterns exerted distinct effects on the dominant taxa of the intestinal microbiota. Under low-temperature conditions, VP-T6a reduced the influence of VP on the microbial network, whereas this effect was absent at high temperatures. Moreover, low-temperature interaction patterns more effectively increased the contribution of deterministic processes in the shrimp intestinal bacterial community compared with high-temperature interaction patterns. This study reveals a temperature-dependent phage-bacterium coexistence strategy in the shrimp intestine that maintains a dynamic equilibrium between phages and their bacterial hosts. At elevated temperatures, phages fail to suppress V. parahaemolyticus proliferation, potentially weakening the intestinal microbiota’s resistance to exogenous invasion and thereby posing a potential risk to digestive tract health in shrimp. Video Abstract

title: Phage-based depletion of Variovorax reveals interactions within intact microbiomes
abstract: Abstract Background Testing microbial interaction hypotheses, including metabolite cross-feeding, remains a major challenge in microbiome research. Phages have the potential to probe organism-organism interactions within complex microbiomes yet are rarely utilised for this purpose. Results Here, we isolated nine narrow host-range phages that replicate in several ecologically important Variovorax species. We used three of the phages to deplete Variovorax SCN45 from complex enrichment communities (containing 18 to 31 species) to test correlation network-based hypothesis of thiamine interdependencies . Genome-resolved metagenomics revealed that a Leifsonia population decreased in relative abundance following Variovorax SCN45 depletion but could be rescued by thiamine supplementation. As a further demonstration of this approach, we used phages to eliminate Variovorax CL14 from a defined rhizosphere co-culture grown with Arabidopsis , where Variovorax CL14 degrades the plant hormone auxin produced by Arthrobacter CL28, and re-established the stunted root phenotype. Conclusion Thus we confirmed thiamine production as the mechanistic basis for interdependence between Variovorax and Leifsonia . These experiments lay the foundation for research that employs wildtype and engineered phages to test interaction hypotheses and for targeted microbiome manipulation.

title: SCiMS: Sex Calling in Metagenomic Sequences
abstract: Abstract Background Host sex is a critical determinant of microbial community structure across many host species, influenced by hormonal profiles, physiology, and sex-stratified behaviors. Despite its importance, sex metadata is frequently missing in microbiome studies, including animal-associated samples. Host chromosomal sex can be inferred from the host-derived reads present in metagenomic data, but existing genomic sex prediction tools rely on fixed coverage thresholds calibrated for human XY chromosomes and require relatively high numbers of host reads, limiting their use on low host-biomass samples such as stool and on organisms with other sex-determination systems. Results Here, we present SCiMS (Sex Calling in Metagenomic Sequences), a bioinformatic tool that leverages host-derived DNA within shotgun metagenomic data to predict host chromosomal sex, even at low host coverage. SCiMS uses a multinomial likelihood computed from observed read counts under each sex and reports chromosomal sex calls. Because the expected read distribution is derived directly from chromosome lengths and ploidy under each candidate karyotype, SCiMS applies to any organism with a heterogametic sex-determination system. We benchmarked SCiMS against existing tools on simulated metagenomic data, human metagenomic samples spanning multiple body sites, and metagenomic samples from seven animal species. SCiMS matched or outperformed existing tools, with a noticeable advantage at low host read conditions. Conclusions SCiMS provides an accurate, scalable, and generalizable solution for host chromosomal sex classification across host species, even when host DNA is minimal. By enabling recovery of missing sex metadata, it serves as a quality-control tool for analyses in microbiome research. SCiMS is freely available at https://github.com/davenport-lab/SCiMS .

title: Gut microbiota-derived phenylalanine metabolites exacerbate elderly-onset acute pancreatitis by promoting mitophagy and enhancing cell death
abstract: Elderly-onset acute pancreatitis (EOAP) shows increased severity and mortality, yet the age-related mechanisms underlying its pathogenesis remain incompletely understood. Here, we define the role of gut microbiota dysbiosis in enhancing the severity of EOAP through altered phenylalanine (PA) metabolism. Aged mice and elderly patients displayed elevated phenaceturic acid (PAC) and phenylacetylglutamine (PG), along with increased Escherichia-Shigella abundance. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from aged donors reproduced the aggravated inflammatory phenotype in young recipient mice. Mechanistically, PAC compromises mitochondrial integrity and induces apoptosis, thereby enhancing inflammatory responses. Our findings highlight dysregulated apoptosis and mitochondrial homeostasis as underlying mechanisms contributing to EOAP severity, and suggest that targeting microbial PA metabolism may offer a novel therapeutic avenue for EOAP. Video Abstract

title: Antibody-mediated immune surveillance as an organizing axis of gut microbiota structure
abstract: Abstract Background The symbiotic interplay between the immune system and the endogenous microbiome is essential for maintaining homeostasis. However, most microbiome research focuses primarily on associations between disease and microbial composition, often overlooking host–microbiota interactions as a defining component of health and pathology. The gut microbiota is continuously monitored by the immune system, particularly via immunoglobulin A (IgA), which shapes microbial communities by selectively targeting specific taxa. Despite its central role, IgA-mediated immune surveillance has rarely been formalized as a quantitative axis in microbiota analysis, limiting our understanding of how host–microbe interactions influence health and disease. Results We developed an immune-informed framework to quantify IgA-mediated microbial engagement using the Species Immune Engagement Score (IM score ). IM score integrates three key features: IgA binding to each microbe, microbial abundance, and prevalence across individuals, producing a quantitative measure of how actively the immune system targets each taxon. Applying IM score across three geographically distinct cohorts, we identified a conserved set of IgA-targeted gut microbes. This includes well-characterized commensals, such as Coprococcus comes and uncharacterized taxa (e.g . , Oscillospiraceae SGB15216), highlighting microbes that are immunologically relevant but often overlooked. In early multiple sclerosis (MS), IM score revealed a profound fragmentation of IgA-mediated immune engagement, particularly among short-chain fatty acid–producing bacteria and dominant archaeal lineage. These patterns are not captured by standard diversity or compositional metrics. To capture community-level organization, we aggregated IM score values into the Immunologically Engaged Gut Microbiota Index (IMG index ). Using IMG index , we tracked disruptions in IgA-mediated immune engagement in early MS and observed its sensitivity to changes following fecal microbiota transplantation and fluctuations in disease activity. This demonstrates the potential of IMG index to monitor both disease-associated alterations and therapeutic responses. Conclusion These findings establish IgA-mediated immune surveillance as a quantifiable axis of gut microbiota organization, providing an ecological framework for understanding host–microbe interactions.

title: Integrative characterization of host–microbiome-diet axes during early-life development of the murine gut
abstract: Abstract Background Early-life development of the gut microbiome plays a critical role in shaping host physiology. However, a comprehensive understanding of how diet, microbial community assembly, functional capacity, and host intestinal maturation axes evolve and coordinate over time remains lacking. Most studies focus on a single axis, rely on cross-sectional sampling, or have limited functional resolution, restricting insight into developmental dynamics. Here, we characterized early-life maturation of the gut ecosystem using longitudinal, metaproteome-level analysis in a murine model. Results Using metaproteomics, we profiled fecal samples collected at seven postnatal time points from day 10 to weaning and into early adulthood (day 48) in pups from two contemporaneously raised C57BL/6 cohorts differing only in maternal origin (a long-established local colony and newly purchased pregnant females from the same vendor). Analyses accounted for time, cohort, and sex effects. Microbial communities underwent pronounced taxonomic succession, shifting from early dominance by facultative anaerobes to obligate anaerobes after weaning, accompanied by increasing species richness and functional complexity across cohorts and sexes. Taxonomic changes were co-occurring with an increase in functional redundancy that converged by postnatal day 34 and remained stable into early adulthood. KEGG clustering revealed patterns consistent with changes in metabolic pathway representation alongside maintenance of core functions. Direct detection of low-abundant dietary proteins provided evidence for dietary transitions coinciding with microbial maturation: milk proteins were detected only before weaning, while solid food components predominated over time. Maternal origin was significantly associated with microbial engraftment trajectories, leading to cohort-specific taxonomic and functional differences despite identical housing and diet. In parallel, host intestinal proteome maturation mirrored microbial succession, with concomitant shifts in metabolic, absorptive, regulatory, and effector pathways, including antimicrobial peptides and carbohydrate-modifying enzymes. Conclusions By directly integrating microbial, dietary, functional, and host axes within a longitudinal framework, this study provides a comprehensive view of murine gut ecosystem maturation during early life and offers a reference for interpreting developmental microbiome dynamics and improving experimental design and reproducibility in mouse studies.

title: Vegans have distinct profiles of their gut microbiome and multi-compartment metabolome that align with markers of metabolic health
abstract: Adherence to a vegan diet is associated with improved cardiometabolic health. Here, we relate the outcome of shotgun sequencing of faecal DNA, serum, faecal and urine metabolomics, and systemic cytokine profiling with measures of clinical and biochemical markers of cardiometabolic health in 75 vegans and 75 omnivores without known diseases. Compared with omnivorous, the diet of vegans was enriched in fibres and digestible carbohydrates and lower in protein and fat. Vegans displayed favourable cardiometabolic phenotypes including lower measures of glycaemia, atherogenic plasma lipids and systemic inflammation. Despite a lower alpha-diversity, the vegan gut bacteriome exhibited distinct signatures with an enrichment of bacterial taxa that associated directly with intake of dietary fibres, and which were positively linked to health-related cardiometabolic scores based on the ZOE Microbiome Ranking 2024. In addition, within vegans, measures of bacterial diversity correlated positively with dietary protein intake. Omnivore-enriched bacterial species that associated with favourable metabolic health outcomes according to the ZOE ranking were also enriched in those vegans who had a high-protein intake compared to vegans with a low-protein intake. Further, the vegan gut microbiome was featured by a lower abundance of virulent bacteriophages and viral auxiliary metabolic genes as well as a higher prevalence of the eukaryotic Blastocystis protist that associated with a lower systolic blood pressure. In omnivores, the abundance of several gut bacteriome-derived metabolites including trimethylamine-N-oxide and p -cresyl sulphate associated with markers of adverse metabolic and renal outcomes. We show how a vegan diet is associated with a coordinated restructuring of the gut bacteriome, virome, Blastocystis prevalence and the multi-component metabolome, findings that provide insights into potential mechanisms underlying the associations between diet and human cardiometabolic health. Video Abstract

title: Novel Antarctic chemolithotroph drives iron biomineralization
abstract: BACKGROUND: Iron, the most abundant redox-active metal in the Earth's crust, is coupled to numerous biogeochemical cycles. However, the mechanisms of iron oxidation and the organisms involved remain incompletely understood. Banded iron formations (BIFs) are a major reservoir of iron ore in the Precambrian sedimentary record, yet the biological contribution to their genesis remains a subject of unresolved debate. While large-scale BIF deposition largely ceased after the Proterozoic, microbial activity in modern Holocene sediments under fluctuating redox conditions provides a unique opportunity to examine mechanisms reminiscent of ancient iron cycling. Here, we report the stratigraphic sequence of microbiome profiles recorded in laminated facies with iron-containing crystalline illite in the embayment sediments beneath the Larsen C Ice Shelf (LCIS) in Antarctica during the Holocene. RESULTS: LCIS sediments record microbial community shifts tightly coupled to environmental changes throughout the Holocene. Metagenomic analyses revealed three dominant microbial phases corresponding to geological facies boundaries. The open marine setting (phase A) showed higher taxonomic richness, whereas the sub-ice shelf sediments (phases B and C) were largely anoxic and characterized by diverse chemolithoautotrophic metabolisms. Keystone taxa including uncultured members of Thermodesulfovibrionia, as well as unique microbial communities and metabolisms, were evident in the aphotic, anoxic seawater; metagenomic analyses further revealed chemolithotrophy. The Thermodesulfovibrionia bacterium, visualized using fluorescence in situ hybridization and designated as "Candidatus Mariimomonas ferrooxydans", formed a novel clade in the phylum Nitrospirota. Metagenome-assembled genome analysis identified a putative outer-membrane Fe(II) oxidase, Cyc2, whose Fe(II)-oxidation activity was experimentally confirmed. CONCLUSION: Our findings document the interaction between microbiome and environment, illustrating how LCIS sediments preserve a dynamic record of microbial community responses to environmental transitions. These results provide critical insights into microbial iron mineralization, echoing the biogeochemistry of the geologic past, particularly synglacial iron formation during the Neoproterozoic Snowball Earth. Video Abstract.

title: The PSR signaling pathway facilitates enrichment of P-solubilizing Burkholderia to enhance P acquisition in soybean
abstract: Abstract Background Association with beneficial microbes is essential for plants maintaining fitness under biotic or abiotic stress. Mechanisms underlying this call for community support, and the species involved, remain largely unknown. Results We revealed that the phosphate starvation response (PSR) pathway contributes to enrich the phosphate solubilizing bacteria (PSB) Burkholderia for better P acquisition in soybean. We discovered that P deficiency significantly increased the relative abundance of Burkholderia in soybean roots and rhizospheres in field trials. Constitutively activation of the PSR pathway through overexpression of GmPHR33 significantly enhanced root-associated compartments with Burkholderia , while repression through knockout of GmPHR33 repressed it. Furthermore, the PSR pathway appeared to regulate malate exudation to enrich PSB, while the GmPHR33-GmALMT29 module was revealed as a mediator of the malate exudation process. Conclusions Our results uncovered a novel mechanism utilized by legumes to enrich functional microbes that can help legumes cope with P deficiency. The mechanism elucidated in this work acts through activation of the PSR signaling pathway under P deficiency conditions, which enriches PSB, particularly Burkholderia, for support in acquiring P.

title: Comparative genomics and super-resolution microscopy of novel cyanophages reveals genomic isomerism, auxiliary genes, and a non-synchronous infection process
abstract: Abstract Background Microbial communities of multicellular, heterocyst-forming cyanobacteria assimilate organic nitrogen from dinitrogen gas through nitrogen fixation and are important photosynthetic primary producers. This makes them ecologically significant, particularly in freshwater, wetlands, and agricultural ecosystems. Cyanophages, viruses that specifically infect cyanobacteria play a key role in lysing them, terminating cyanobacterial blooms, and turning over the nutrients accumulated by these communities, with tremendous relevance for the biogeochemical cycles in these environments. However, only a limited number of cyanophages infecting N 2 -fixing cyanobacteria have been genome sequenced to date, and it has remained unknown how their interaction proceeds with the individual cells within the filaments forming the backbone of these communities. Results We isolated and characterized three Caudoviricetes cyanophages (A-Lf14, A-Alj1, and A-Hlh1) specifically infecting the N 2 -fixing cyanobacterium Anabaena sp. PCC 7120. Super-resolution microscopy revealed heterogeneous infection outcomes among adjacent cells within individual host filaments, indicating asynchronous infection progression at the single-cell level. Comparative genomics revealed a conserved ~30 kb invertible genomic region flanked by inverted repeats, a structural configuration with limited precedent in cyanophages. Using diagnostic PCR, Sanger sequencing, and read-mapping, we validated that two isomers stably coexist within phage populations. In contrast to the previously characterized cyanophage A-1(L), the three new phages encode a non-cyanobacterial alkaline phosphatase (PhoD). The expression of phoD was highly upregulated during infection, suggesting a phage-driven mechanism for phosphorus acquisition. Conversely, these phages lack the early-expressed tnpB endonuclease gene carried by A-1(L). Transcription of tnpB was strongly upregulated for both strands ( tnpB fwd and tnpB rev ) during A-1(L) infection, while infection by the three novel phages modestly induced the transcription of five identical host-encoded tnpB copies. In a highly unusual setting, both tnpB strands are protein-coding over their entire length, leading to the expression of a 347-residue protein from the tnpB rev strand. Conclusions This study reveals that genomic isomerism is a source of structural plasticity in freshwater cyanophages and uncovers functionally distinct auxiliary gene repertoires that link phage infection strategies to nutrient status. Our findings provide mechanistic insight into how cyanophages diversify their genomes, interact with their hosts and show that a phage gene can be protein-coding on both strands.

title: A GacS-mediated regulatory framework coordinates bacterial competition and rhizosphere microbiome remodeling in Pseudomonas fluorescens
abstract: Plant growth-promoting Pseudomonas bacteria are promising biocontrol agents whose regulatory and effector genes shape bacterial traits involved in interactions with host plants and soil microorganisms. However, previous research has predominantly examined individual genes or traits in isolation, often making it difficult to compare their relative contributions within a single strain. This reductionist approach limits our understanding of how beneficial bacteria simultaneously engage in interactions with plants, suppress pathogens, and shape microbial communities. To address this gap, we selected 16 representative genes and gene clusters in P. fluorescens 2P24 based on genome annotation and previous knowledge of three PGPR-relevant functional layers: protein secretion systems, regulatory pathways, and secondary metabolite biosynthesis. This panel included the major annotated protein secretion systems in strain 2P24, selected regulatory systems with known or predicted roles in bacterial physiology and ecological interactions, and secondary-metabolite-related genes/gene clusters such as phl (2,4-DAPG biosynthetic gene cluster). We then examined how deletion of these genes or gene clusters affected bacterial traits, plant immune elicitation, and soil or rhizosphere bacterial community composition. Through comprehensive genetic and phenotypic analyses, we identified six genes and gene clusters— lapBCE , gacS , phoP , rsmX , fliC , and phl —that are essential for fundamental bacterial physiological processes and ecological fitness. More importantly, we discovered two regulatory modules, GacS-Phl and GacS-FliC, that coordinately govern multi-interface ecological interactions in the rhizosphere. Specifically, GacS regulates the production of 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol, an antimicrobial compound that directly suppresses competing soil-dwelling Streptomyces populations. Simultaneously, GacS modulates flagellin expression, and flagellin acts as a microbe-associated molecular pattern triggering plant immune responses that indirectly reshape the composition and structure of rhizosphere microbiome communities. This study establishes a coordinated regulatory model that integrates global regulatory networks, microbe-associated molecular patterns, and antimicrobial secondary metabolites in mediating complex ecological interactions. Our findings reveal that beneficial Pseudomonas strains employ a GacS-mediated regulatory framework to simultaneously manage multiple ecological interfaces, providing mechanistic insights into how these bacteria balance plant-beneficial activities with competitive strategies. This regulatory framework offers a theoretical foundation for rational design and application of microbial biocontrol agents for sustainable agricultural practices. Video Abstract

title: Underexplored diversity and transmission of RNA viruses in Antarctic aquatic animals
abstract: Antarctic extreme environmental conditions harbor unique ecosystems with underexplored viral diversity. While viruses in Antarctic mammals and birds have been previously documented, the viromes of ecologically pivotal aquatic species, such as Antarctic krill ( Euphausia superba ), remain largely unknown. Here, we characterize RNA viromes from Antarctic species employing metatranscriptomic sequencing of 403 samples collected from the seas near the Antarctic Peninsula and South Shetland Islands, the South Orkney Islands, and South Georgia Island (all in Western Antarctica), and the Cosmonauts Sea (Eastern Antarctica) during 2019–2024. We identified 58 RNA viruses across 19 families/clades, including positive-sense, single-stranded RNA ( n = 37), negative-sense, single-stranded RNA ( n = 5), and double-stranded RNA ( n = 16) viruses. A total of 51 viruses (88%) were novel, revealing extensive hidden viral diversity in Antarctic animals. We performed α- and β-diversity analyses which revealed that host specificity significantly shaped virome composition, while the influence of geographic location warranted further study. Notably, we detected near-identical strains of Lawrence virus (99.35% RdRp identity), Vespucci virus (97.70–99.08%), and a picornavirus in Antarctic krill/fish and their predators, the chinstrap penguin ( Pygoscelis antarcticus ) and the Antarctic fur seal ( Arctocephalus gazella ), suggestive of potential cross-species transmission through food chains. Our findings reveal previously underexplored virome diversity in Antarctic aquatic ecosystems, underscore the evolutionary adaptability of RNA viruses in extreme habitats, and provide essential data for biosecurity assessments concerning the potential movement of viral pathogens in polar and connected ecosystems. Video Abstract

title: Salivary prognostic bacterial signatures associated with survival outcomes and recurrence risk in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Abstract Background Alterations in the oral microbiota are increasingly recognized as an integral component of the tumor microenvironment, forming a clinically relevant oncobiome that may modulate tumorigenesis, therapeutic response, and patient prognosis in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Methods In this prospective study, we characterized the salivary microbiome of 124 Spanish HNSCC patients (86 laryngeal and 38 pharyngeal carcinomas) and 66 healthy controls from northern Spain using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Microbial community structure, differential abundance, and associations with tumor site and treatment received were analyzed using ANCOM-BC, while prognostic associations were assessed through univariable and multivariable Cox regression models and survival analyses. Results Distinct microbial community profiles were observed between patients and controls, revealing pronounced site-specific dysbiosis between pharyngeal and laryngeal tumors. Microbiome composition also varied according to treatment modality. Chemoradiotherapy induced a marked remodeling of the oncobiome, characterized by a post-treatment enrichment of Lactobacillus . More importantly, a specific 10-bacteria salivary signature was significantly associated with poorer survival outcomes. including disease-specific survival (DSS), overall survival (OS), and disease-free survival (DFS). This 10-bacterial signature remained independently associated with poor prognosis in multivariable analysis for DSS (HR = 6.215; p < 0.001), OS (HR = 5.417; p < 0.001), and DFS (HR = 6.842; p < 0.001), after adjustment for established clinicopathological variables. Furthermore, we identified tumor site–specific prognostic taxa within the oral microbiome of HNSCC patients. The presence of putative Prevotella , Porphyromonas and Fusobacterium species specifically and significantly correlated with improved DSS, OS and DFS in pharyngeal carcinomas, whereas putative Stomatobaculum longum and Dialister were associated with favorable survival outcomes in laryngeal carcinomas. Conclusions Our findings reveal distinct oral microbial patterns linked to HNSCC prognosis and recurrence risk, demonstrating that the salivary microbiome may represent a source of non-invasive, dynamic biomarkers for risk stratification and personalized management. The identification of tumor site–specific bacterial signatures associated with both favorable and unfavorable survival outcomes supports the concept of an anatomically contextualized oncobiome, although validation in independent cohorts and higher-resolution microbiome studies will be required before clinical implementation.

title: Defining the genomic and ecological landscapes of the human anellome
abstract: Human anelloviruses (ANVs) represent one of the most diverse, prevalent, and persistent viral communities within the human virome and constitute dominant members of the commensal viral ecosystem. Despite their ubiquity and emerging associations with immune modulation and hematologic malignancy, the genomic diversity and community organization of the human ANV virome (anellome) remain incompletely resolved. This limitation is driven in part by fragmented reference datasets, inconsistent taxonomic annotation, and geographic underrepresentation, particularly for Asian populations. A geographically expanded reference and standardized analytical framework are therefore needed to profile the human anellome at species-level and lineage-level resolution. We integrated metagenomic sequencing data from 6348 Chinese samples with globally available ANV genomes to construct an expanded phylogenomic resource for the human anellome. This integration improved Asian representation and expanded represented human ANV diversity to 771 species-level taxa, comprising 91 ICTV-recognized human-associated species and 680 provisional new species (PNS), corresponding to an approximately eightfold expansion in represented species-level diversity. The resulting framework enabled high-resolution profiling of personal anellomes. The richest individual profile contained 305 species-level taxa and 2071 lineages, indicating extensive intra-host ANV diversity under the expanded reference framework. Across analyzed cohorts and public metadata, we identified recurrent core anellome components characterized by high detection frequency, abundance, geographic representation, cross-cohort reproducibility, and longitudinal persistence. Several core lineages showed significant inverse associations with CD4 T-cell counts in HIV-infected individuals. Paired peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) and plasma analyses further identified compartment-associated differences in diversity, composition, and lineage enrichment. Within this framework, a TTMV::RARA -associated Betatorquevirus clade showed higher ORF2 conservation, RUNX1 motif enrichment, and PBMC-biased distribution compared with background clades. These findings support the human anellome as a structured commensal viral community that can be resolved at species-level and lineage-level resolution. The HANVdb Resource provides a reusable framework for investigating ANV diversity, anellome ecology, immune-associated variation, compartmental organization, and lineage-level hypotheses relevant to viral integration-associated disease. Video Abstract

title: Using the housekeeping gene cpn60 as a marker for microbial community profiling and viability assessment
abstract: Abstract High-throughput sequencing has revolutionized microbiome research, yet distinguishing viable from nonviable microbes in complex communities remains challenging. Microbial viability underlines microbiome function, which is mostly driven by living, active members. Transcriptional activity of genes has been suggested as a viability marker but not systematically explored in complex communities. Here, we find that both community-wide transcription and cpn60 gene activity can effectively quantify community composition and identify viable members. For targeted cpn60 amplicons, protein-coding RNA activity better captured the differential structure of the active community than 16S rRNA amplicons. To enable scalable application, we constructed an expanded database integrating diverse cpn60 protein and nucleotide sequences, substantially extending the existing cpnDB database. In Human Microbiome Project II data, cpn60 protein-based taxonomy strongly agreed with shotgun metagenomic profiles. C pn60 transcript abundance correlated positively with bacterial growth rates estimated by the bPTR method, indicating its potential as a marker of microbial transcriptional activity and viability. It also distinguished resident gut microbes from potentially transient (e.g., oral-typical) members. Together, these results demonstrate that integrating DNA and RNA sequences at the single cpn60 locus enables accurate profiling of microbiome composition and activity, offering a cost-effective framework extendable to other rationally selected genes across diverse ecosystems.

title: Clostridium butyricum and butyrate reprogram macrophages to alleviate obesity by disrupting the LPS-EGR1 axis and its associated PI3K-Akt signaling
abstract: Obesity is closely associated with gut microbial dysbiosis and chronic low-grade inflammation, yet how microbial signals orchestrate systemic immune-metabolic dysfunction remains unclear. In adiposity-prone Ningxiang pigs (NF), we observed an expansion of Gram-negative bacteria, elevated circulating lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and reduced abundance of Clostridium butyricum and its metabolite butyrate. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from NF donors induced adiposity in lean Duroc-Landrace-Yorkshire (CF) recipients, accompanied by a significant decrease in C. butyricum colonization. In high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice, supplementation with C. butyricum and butyrate effectively restored gut microbial homeostasis and ameliorated obesity. Integrated multi-organ transcriptomic analyses across pigs and long-tailed macaques revealed that early growth response 1 ( EGR1 ) is a central regulator of obesity-associated inflammation, with consistent enrichment of PI3K-Akt signaling. Single-cell RNA sequencing further demonstrated that EGR1 -high macrophages adopt a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype, whereas EGR1 -low macrophages exhibit an anti-inflammatory M2 profile. Leveraging EGR1 macrophage-specific differentially expressed genes, both in silico knockout of EGR1 and pharmacological inhibition (EGR1i; IT25) confirmed the functional involvement of PI3K-Akt signaling downstream of EGR1 . Integrating metagenomic and single-cell data, we propose a conserved LPS- EGR1 axis that governs macrophage polarization in obesity. To experimentally validate this model, we established an LPS-potentiated HFD-induced obesity model in mice and an LPS-induced M1 polarization model in RAW264.7 macrophages. Treatment with C. butyricum , butyrate, arginine, or EGR1i significantly attenuated weight gain, downregulated EGR1 expression, and effectively suppressed M1 macrophage polarization, thereby restoring the M1/M2 balance. Notably, this process is accompanied by significant alterations in genes related to the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, suggesting that this pathway may act in concert with EGR1 within this regulatory network. In summary, these cross-species experiments elucidate a fundamental mechanism whereby gut-derived LPS regulates macrophage polarization via EGR1 , thereby linking microbial dysbiosis to metabolic inflammation in mammals. Video Abstract CB and BA break the LPS-EGR1-M1 loop to combat obesity. CB: Clostridium butyricum. BA: Butyric acid. LPS: Lipopolysaccharide. GNB: Gram-negative bacteria. EGR1: Early Growth Response 1.

title: Volatile-mediated microbiome enrichment by Streptomyces albidoflavus G1 enhances suppression of apple ring rot pathogen Botryosphaeria dothidea
abstract: Abstract Background Apple ring rot, caused by the fungal pathogen Botryosphaeria dothidea , is a devastating disease affecting apple production. It causes extensive damage to fruit and branches, leading to significant economic losses within the apple industry in China and across the globe. While the volatile organic compound G1-VOC has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in suppressing B. dothidea and reducing fruit decay, its internal biocontrol mechanism and the host transcriptional response remain largely unexplored. Results This study integrated microbiome analysis, VOC-bacterial interaction studies, and transcriptome profiling to investigate the mechanism by which G1-VOCs regulates apple endophytes to suppress apple ring rot. Initially, G1 was identified for its VOC-mediated biocontrol activity. GC-MS analysis showed compounds from sesquiterpenoid, triterpenoid, and phenylalanine metabolism pathways act as primary inhibitors, disrupting fungal glycolysis, membrane integrity, and biofilm formation. 16S rRNA analysis revealed G1-VOCs prevent bacterial diversity imbalances caused by Staphylococcus during infection while maintaining microbial stability by regulating Pseudomonas abundance and recruiting the antagonistic strain Pseudomonas sp. aNRL1. Interactions between G1-VOCs and aNRL1 suggested the volatiles modulate bacterial growth kinetics, biofilm formation and motility to favour antagonistic strain. Finally, transcriptome analysis demonstrated G1 treatment reactivates the Brassinosteroid signaling pathway and upregulates genes associated with the MAPK cascade, lipid metabolism, and cuticle/wax biosynthesis during pathogen challenge. Conclusion G1-VOCs regulate microbial composition in apple endophytic tissues by enriching antagonistic strain and reprogram the apple transcriptome by upregulating defence and signalling pathways to counteract B. dothidea.

title: Lesion-anchored viromics identifies candidate viral agents of broiler stunting diseases
abstract: Abstract Background Broiler stunting diseases, including malabsorption-associated runting-stunting syndrome (RSS) and maldigestion-associated transmissible viral proventriculitis (TVP), cause significant economic losses through growth failure and increased mortality. Viral infections have been proposed as contributors, yet the aetiological roles of specific viruses remain obscure because conventional virome studies lack spatial resolution and cannot distinguish which viruses localise to lesion sites versus unaffected tissues. This limits inference regarding direct viral involvement in pathogenesis. Methods We developed a spatially informed viromic approach by coupling laser-capture microdissection of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissues (duodenum, jejunum, proventriculus and gizzard) with metatranscriptomic sequencing, enabling viral communities within histological lesions to be compared with those in unaffected non-lesion regions of the same birds and flocks. Candidate viruses identified by sequencing were then verified in matched fresh-frozen tissues from the same birds by RT-PCR, RT-qPCR, amplicon sequencing, and virus isolation. Results In RSS-derived laser-microdissected samples ( n = 71), three enteric viruses were consistently enriched within gastrointestinal lesion tissues relative to non-lesion tissues: the species Gallivirus spp. (multiple strains), Avastrovirus galli , and Rotavirus deltagastroenteritidis. These viruses were detected across multiple affected farms, with co-occurrence in individual lesion samples suggesting potential co-infections. Comparative analysis with TVP-derived laser-microdissected samples ( n = 49) revealed distinct enteric virome compositions between the two syndromes, with differential enrichment of vaccine-like strains in TVP, confirming that this spatially informed approach can discriminate disease-specific viral signatures. All three RSS candidates were independently confirmed in matched fresh-frozen tissue homogenates from the same birds, and chicken astrovirus was recovered in cell culture. Conclusions By anchoring virome composition directly to lesion histopathology, we identified candidate viral agents associated with RSS pathogenesis and demonstrated that spatially informed viromics moves beyond conventional virome surveys by linking viral abundance patterns to histopathological context. This framework provides a foundation for investigating whether these candidate viruses function as primary pathogens or co-factors in stunting disease development.

title: The plant-beneficial fungus Gongronella butleri w5 reallocates plant-derived sucrose to enrich IAA-producing bacteria to promote plant root development in phosphorus-rich soil
abstract: Mucoromycotina fungi are known to enhance plant performance under nutrient-deficient conditions by restructuring rhizosphere microbial communities and mobilizing soil nutrients. However, their functional roles in nutrient-rich soils remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether the plant-beneficial fungus Gongronella butleri w5 (w5) can promote the growth of Solanum lycopersicum under phosphorus-rich conditions and explored the underlying tripartite interactions among plants, fungi, and bacteria. Greenhouse experiments, soil microcosm analyses, high-throughput sequencing, functional assays, and host-induced gene silencing revealed that w5 significantly enhanced plant biomass, root development, and photosynthetic efficiency despite not altering soil nutrient availability. w5 inoculation reshaped the rhizosphere microbiome, enriching indole-3-acetic acid (IAA)-producing bacterial taxa. Bacillus megaterium and Bacillus zanthoxyli , identified as key IAA producers, were isolated from the w5 hyphosphere. Tripartite interaction assays showed that w5 imports plant-derived sucrose through the transporter GspSUT1, hydrolyzes it into glucose and fructose, and releases these hexoses into the rhizosphere, thereby facilitating bacterial colonization and enhancing IAA biosynthesis. Silencing GspSUT1 significantly impaired hexose secretion and subsequent bacterial IAA production, thereby disrupting the synergistic plant growth promotion effect. Our findings reveal a carbon-driven mechanism by which Mucoromycotina fungi establish a metabolic niche to drive synergistic plant development in nutrient-rich soils. By acting as an ecological “invertase” to reallocate plant sucrose into hexoses, w5 enriches IAA-producing bacteria. This carbon-hormone coupling synergistically improves root architecture, photosynthetic capacity, and nutrient uptake. These insights highlight the functional plasticity of Mucoromycotina fungi in shaping rhizosphere microbiomes and their potential as sustainable biological inputs. Video Abstract

title: Exploring the biogeographical patterns and driving mechanisms of microbial communities in four microhabitats of Zostera japonica beds
abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution patterns and driving mechanisms of plant-associated microbial communities across multiple scales is essential for uncovering the generation and maintenance of microbial diversity under plant influence. However, large-scale evidence on the biogeographical patterns of seagrass-associated microbes remains scarce. Here, we sequenced microbial communities in four microhabitats (seawater, phyllosphere, rhizosphere, and sediment) of Zostera japonica beds in China, generating 480 amplicon sequencing datasets and 40 metagenomes. Subsequent analysis explored the structure and functional potential of microbial communities in these microhabitats. The microbial community exhibits significant spatial distribution patterns, characterized by latitudinal distribution patterns and distance decay relationships. While the null model results suggest a dominance of random processes in the construction of microbial communities in Zostera japonica beds, NST analysis reveals a transition from stochasticity to determinism in the assembly of rhizosphere bacterial communities with increasing latitude. Response ratio and GAM analysis further demonstrate differential responses of bacterial and fungal communities to environmental factors, indicating selective regulation of microbial groups by specific environmental drivers in different microhabitats. Functional analysis reveals that key genes involved in nitrogen and sulfur metabolism (such as nirS , norBC , cysNDCH , and cysJI ) display latitudinal gradient changes and microhabitat-specific differences in annotated microbes. For example, the cysC gene found in northern sampling points is sourced from Actinomycetota, Bacteridota, and Cyanobacteriota, while in southern sampling points, it primarily comes from Campylobacterota and Pseudomonadota, highlighting the functional adaptability of microbes to environmental heterogeneity. As the first systematic investigation into the biogeographic patterns of microbial communities associated with marine macrophytes, this study not only elucidates the multi-scale distribution patterns of Zostera japonica bed microbiomes but also establishes a theoretical framework for the dual regulation of microbial communities by latitude and microhabitat. The discoveries provide new insights into further investigating the interactions between microbes and seagrasses, as well as the potential for biogeochemical cycling. They contribute to understanding the adaptive strategies of seagrass ecosystems under different environmental pressures and how microbial communities respond to these stressors. This information is crucial for assessing the health of seagrass beds, predicting their response to environmental changes, and formulating effective conservation and management measures based on scientific evidence. Video Abstract

title: Longitudinal strain-level metagenomics reveals reciprocal Lactobacillus dynamics and outcome-associated protein variants during IVF treatment
abstract: The vaginal microbiome influences reproductive outcomes, yet strain-level dynamics during assisted reproductive treatment remain unexplored. Existing studies rely on species-level resolution that cannot distinguish within-species functional heterogeneity, leaving mechanistic questions unanswered. We conducted longitudinal shotgun metagenomic sequencing of vaginal samples from 41 women undergoing IVF/ICSI treatment across six timepoints (pre-stimulation baseline through pregnancy testing; 186 samples total). Strain-level analysis using inStrain revealed that Lactobacillus crispatus genomic stability and Lactobacillus iners adaptive flexibility both associate with pregnancy success, representing a reciprocal dynamic pattern. Functional protein analysis identified two outcome-associated targets: Inerolysin, a cholesterol-dependent cytolysin from L. iners , and L-lactate dehydrogenase (L-LDH) from L. crispatus . Structural modeling suggested that the Success-specific Inerolysin S429P mutation is predicted to disrupt cholesterol-binding, potentially attenuating cytolytic activity, while the L-LDH P169L mutation may enhance catalytic efficiency. Four orthogonal computational methods (FoldX thermodynamic calculation, ESM-1v evolutionary scoring, ConSurf conservation analysis, and 10 ns molecular dynamics simulation) provided convergent computational evidence supporting these structural interpretations. Critically, these protective variants were enriched at baseline (T1) rather than arising during treatment, indicating that pre-existing strain genetics predispose to differential responses under hormonal stress. A baseline 18-SNV prediction panel achieved an internal cross-validation AUC of 0.945 and an external validation AUC of 0.784 in an independent cohort ( n = 69) sequenced on a multiplex amplicon PCR platform. These findings reveal strain-level functional variants as candidate mechanistic determinants of reproductive success and potential biomarkers for personalized risk assessment in ART. The reciprocal dynamics of L. crispatus stability and L. iners adaptive flexibility, together with the dual-protein mutation pattern, suggest targets for strain-specific probiotic interventions. All computational predictions require experimental validation through biochemical and functional assays. Video Abstract

title: IgG coating of Lactobacillus crispatus is associated with cervicovaginal immune homeostasis and reduced preterm birth rates, identifying S-layer proteins as candidate antibody targets
abstract: Abstract Background Maternal host immune system responses to cervicovaginal microbiota influence the risk of microbial-driven spontaneous preterm birth (sPTB). Immunoglobulins are present in cervicovaginal fluid (CVF). There are decreased IgG concentrations in women with CST I compared to CST IV, but their role in sPTB is unclear. Here, we investigate immunoglobulin coating of vaginal bacteria in 100 women at high-risk of sPTB (48 sPTB vs 53 term). Results Lactobacillus -dominated communities, especially L. crispatus -dominated, had higher proportions of IgG coating than high diversity, Lactobacillus -depleted communities. There was a positive correlation between IgG and IgG2 coating, indicating IgG2 was the main bound subclass. The percentage of bacterial coating by IgG and IgG2 was higher in women who delivered at term compared to preterm, and IgG coating negatively correlated with concentrations of CVF pro-inflammatory immune mediators. IgG and IgG2 both bound to L. crispatus surface layer proteins (SLPs), identifying SLPs as potential targets of antibody binding associated with immune homeostasis and term birth. Conclusions Our results reveal an association between vaginal bacterial antibody coating and mucosal microbe-immune homeostasis with reduced cervicovaginal inflammation and term birth. These represent a potential component of host-microbe interactions associated with pregnancy outcome.

title: Amino acid availability influences Staphylococcus aureus interaction with the nasal microbiota in a strain- and community-specific manner
abstract: Abstract Background Only some individuals carry Staphylococcus aureus in the nose, predisposing them to endogenous infections. While microbial cooperation and competition are known to shape environmental and intestinal microbial communities, their impact on pathogen colonization within the nasal microbiome is largely unknown. Results Using a newly curated nasal strain collection and systematic pairwise interaction analysis, we investigated competitive and collaborative traits between diverse S. aureus strains and nasal communities. Our experiments revealed that nasal species strongly modulate S. aureus growth in a strain- and community-specific manner both in vitro and in gnotobiotic mice. Nutrient-dependent interactions emerged as key drivers. In one example, we found that tyrosine provided by synthetic communities supported proliferation of an auxotrophic S. aureus strain. Screening of a large collection of S. aureus strains identified tyrosine dependency in 8% of strains, with colonization impaired in the absence of supportive communities, indicating broader relevance of this interaction. Conclusions Our findings reveal distinct metabolic adaptations that enable S. aureus to exploit specific features of resident nasal communities, highlighting complex interspecies networks that influence colonization in the human nose. These insights may inform microbiome-editing strategies to displace S. aureus from the nasal niche.

title: Animal markets are associated with elevated viral diversity and virus–host connectivity across wildlife–farm interfaces
abstract: Animal markets represent important interfaces among wildlife, farmed animals, and humans, yet their role in shaping viral diversity, community structure, and cross-host viral sharing remains incompletely understood. We performed metatranscriptomic analysis of 279 samples collected across wild, farm, and market-associated settings in Guangdong Province, China, with the animal-derived samples encompassing 15 host orders. We identified 106 vertebrate-associated viral lineages represented by 259 viral strains, including 19 putative novel viruses representing 13 putative viral lineages. Viral diversity and viral community composition differed significantly among ecological settings, with market-associated samples generally showing higher viral richness and distinct virome structures than wild and farm samples. The higher viral richness observed in market-associated samples remained evident in sensitivity analyses addressing pooled sampling, host composition, and unequal sampling effort. Viral sharing was observed across wild, farm, and market-associated settings, with market-associated host groups showing particularly extensive virus–host connectivity. Network analyses further indicated greater viral connectivity in market-associated settings, with host groups showing higher degree and betweenness centrality and more extensive virus–host associations. In addition, 38 viral sequences representing 13 viral lineages had documented pathogenic relevance based on reported disease associations in humans or other vertebrate hosts. Zoonotic relevance varied among viral lineages and depended on lineage-, subtype-, or genotype-specific evidence, highlighting the importance of distinguishing disease-associated viruses from those with demonstrated zoonotic potential. Animal markets were associated with greater viral diversity, distinct viral community composition, and broader patterns of viral sharing and connectivity, supporting their role as ecological interfaces linking wildlife and farm systems. However, shared detections do not establish the direction or frequency of viral movement, and temporal heterogeneity remains an important consideration. These findings highlight the value of integrated One Health surveillance across wildlife trade and agricultural systems, together with lineage-specific assessment of viruses with potential human-health relevance. Video Abstract

title: Decoding the metagenome of the precious red coral: discovery of a new spirochete lineage and carotenoid-producing bacteria
abstract: Abstract The precious red coral Corallium rubrum is an ecologically and economically iconic Mediterranean octocoral, yet the diversity and functions of its microbiome remain a “blackbox” at the genomic scale. Here, we present a genome-resolved metagenomic analysis of C. rubrum , reconstructing 25 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), including 16 from wild colonies and 9 additional ones from a laboratory colony, to gain insight into the functional potential of its microbiome. Our phylogenomic analysis of the two dominant Spirochaetota symbionts reveals that one of the two symbionts represents a potential novel, previously undescribed lineage, which appears to be exclusively associated with octocoral species. Functional profiling indicates that these Spirochaetota exhibit different metabolic pathways, and are adapted to the symbiotic life, probably representing mutualistic partners for C. rubrum . Their genomes encode biosynthetic pathways of a wide range of essential amino acids and vitamins, and the capacity to ferment sugars to acetate, potentially supplementing host dietary deficiencies. We also identified an interesting symbiont, affiliated with the Qipengyuania genus, that possesses the genomic potential for the biosynthesis of the carotenoid canthaxanthin, one of the main pigments involved in the red color of C. rubrum . The other MAGs encode a wide range of metabolic pathways, especially those linked to nitrogen and sulfur transformations. Our findings suggest potential metabolic interactions between the red coral host and its microbiome. This study offers detailed taxonomic and functional characterization of newly identified octocoral symbionts, establishing a foundation for future investigations into octocoral symbiotic relationships.

title: Comprehensive sequence analysis reveals the vast β-lactam resistome
abstract: Abstract Most antibiotic-resistance genes (ARGs) evolved in environmental microbes long before humanity’s antibiotic breakthrough, and widespread antibiotic use expedited the dissemination of ARGs among clinical pathogens. While widely discussed, the investigation of environmental ARG distributions lacks the scalability and taxonomic information necessary for a comprehensive analysis. Here, we present a global distribution of all five classes of β-lactamases among microbes and environments. We generated a β-lactamase taxonomy-environment map by identifying >113,000 β-lactamases across diverse bacterial phyla and environmental ecosystems. Remarkably abundant, their occurrence is only ∼2.6-fold lower than the essential recA gene in various environmental ecosystems, with particularly strong enrichment in wastewater and plant samples. The enrichment in plant samples implies an environment where the arms race of β-lactam producers and resistant bacteria occurred over millions of years. We uncover the origins of clinically relevant β-lactamases (mainly in ɣ-Proteobacteria) and expand beyond the previously suggested wastewater samples in plant, terrestrial, and other aquatic settings.

title: Intestinal ROS triggers stress-induced dysbiosis by dismantling the hypoxic barrier
abstract: Stress consistently disrupts the vertebrate gut microbiome, leading to negative health outcomes. However, how systemic stress translates into reproducible microbial dysbiosis remains poorly understood. While current research primarily focuses on late-stage compositional shifts, the early biochemical signals and microenvironmental alterations that precede and initiate this structural breakdown represent a critical knowledge gap. Here we show that stress destabilizes the gut microbiome through a cascade initiated by intestinal reactive oxygen species (ROS). In zebrafish, stress rapidly elicits intestinal ROS accumulation in the distal intestine, emerging within hours and preceding any detectable changes in microbial composition. This early oxidative response does not immediately restructure the community but instead induces a functional collapse: anaerobic fermentation is selectively suppressed and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) production sharply declines while community structure remains largely intact. The resulting SCFAs deficit weakens PPARγ-dependent epithelial metabolic programs, diminishes epithelial oxygen consumption, and erodes the physiological hypoxic barrier. Loss of this barrier re-engineers the luminal niche, enabling the relative enrichment of facultative pathobionts. Restoring epithelial bioenergetics or neutralizing intestinal ROS in zebrafish preserves hypoxia and prevents dysbiosis despite continued stress, identifying intestinal ROS as an early initiating signal of stress-induced dysbiosis. In restraint-stressed mice, the same ordered sequence—early ROS elevation, SCFAs decline, hypoxia loss, and the relative enrichment of facultative taxa—is likewise observed, supporting phenotypic and temporal conservation of this cascade. Our findings reveal that stress-induced dysbiosis is not a stochastic microbial drift, but a highly reproducible ecological cascade that is triggered by an early intestinal ROS burst in zebrafish and phenotypically conserved in mice. By shifting the paradigm from late-stage structural dysbiosis to the initial functional and microenvironmental collapse, we identify the maintenance of the intestinal hypoxic barrier as a critical therapeutic target for stress-related microbiome disorders. title: Top-down mining of a lactobacilli-enriched gut niche in Tunchang pigs identifies a host-derived Limosilactobacillus reuteri strain with anti-colitis activity
abstract: The conventional ‘isolate-and-screen’ strategy for probiotic discovery often lacks ecological context, resulting in strains with uncertain safety profiles and unpredictable functional performance. Indigenous pig breeds, particularly those thriving under low-input husbandry conditions, represent underexplored ‘living libraries’ that offer host- and environment-shaped gut niches. Tunchang (TC) pigs, an indigenous breed from Hainan Province in southeastern China, provide a useful model for top-down, ecology-guided mining of host-derived probiotics from native gut niches. By combining cross-sectional age-gradient metagenomics with cross-breed comparisons, we defined a TC-pig gut niche with a lower overall burden of annotated VF/ARG features than that of Duroc × Landrace × Yorkshire (DLY) pigs. Notably, Limosilactobacillus reuteri was consistently detected within a lactobacilli-enriched core microbiota across developmental-stage groups and showed limited associations with annotated VF/ARG features at the community level. This niche was associated with higher relative levels of several host–microbe co-metabolites, including indoleacrylic acid and N-decanoylglycine. Guided by this framework, we isolated a TC pig-derived L. reuteri strain (TC-Lr) and a co-isolated Lactobacillus johnsonii strain (TC-Lj). Targeted profiling of cell-free culture supernatants revealed a distinct tryptophan-associated metabolic profile of these two isolates, with TC-Lr showing higher concentrations of indole-3-lactic acid and tryptophol than TC-Lj. In a mouse model of dextran sulphate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, TC-Lr, but not TC-Lj, alleviated weight loss and disease activity, attenuated colon shortening and reduced inflammation-associated haematological alterations. TC-Lr also partially restored DSS-disrupted colonic metabolism, increasing adenosine while reducing creatinine and histamine levels. These findings support an ecology-guided, top-down framework for prioritising host-derived probiotics from indigenous livestock breeds. They further suggest that the TC pig gut, characterised by a lactobacilli-enriched community and a lower annotated VF/ARG burden at the community level, may serve as an ecological source for prioritising host-derived probiotic candidates.
